prompt: Which of the four questions in this section can Tarefa answer from the metrics tier alone?
hint: The metrics line has no text in it.

choices.text: Whether answers got worse after the system prompt changed in August
choices.why: That needs examples of prompts and replies; counts cannot show a worse answer.

choices.text: What the assistant costs and whether it is getting slower
choices.why: Right: calls, tokens and milliseconds are all the metrics tier holds, and all this question needs.

choices.text: Why the assistant told one particular client something wrong
choices.why: That needs the exact prompt and output, which only the raw tier has.

choices.text: Whether one account is abusing the assistant
choices.why: The metrics are per day and surface, with no account in them.

prompt: Why does the lesson give the raw text the shortest lifetime of the three tiers?
hint: Which questions need text tied to a person, and when do they come up?

choices.text: Raw text takes the most disk space, so it costs the most to keep
choices.why: Disk is cheap; the cost of raw text is what it contains, not its size.

choices.text: The LGPD sets thirty days as the limit for chat transcripts
choices.why: The LGPD sets no number. The purpose sets it, and thirty days is Tarefa's choice.

choices.text: The questions that need text tied to a person are about recent events
choices.why: Right: debugging a reply and investigating abuse both look at the last days or weeks.

choices.text: Replies cannot be compared across model versions once a month has passed
choices.why: Comparing versions is the quality question, and it uses the redacted tier for months.

prompt: Which of these should a call record carry so that a bad reply can be explained later? Choose all that apply.
hint: What changes between two calls, and what is the same on every call?

choices.text: The request id
choices.why: Yes: it is how a complaint is traced to one record.

choices.text: The name of the model
choices.why: Yes: the same prompt can be answered differently by another model.

choices.text: An identifier for the version of the system prompt
choices.why: Yes: the instructions change more often than the model, and the reply depends on them.

choices.text: The full text of the system prompt, on every call
choices.why: Thousands of identical tokens on every record; a version id points at the same text kept once.

choices.text: The client's CPF, so that the account can be found
choices.why: The account id already finds the account, without putting a document number in the log.

prompt: A client types their card's security code into the support chat. How long may the raw tier keep it?
hint: It is not a question of how many days.

choices.text: Thirty days, like everything else in the raw tier's text
choices.why: The raw tier's limit is for text it may keep at all; this is not such text.

choices.text: None: card rules forbid keeping it after authorisation
choices.why: Right: the PCI DSS forbids keeping it after authorisation, encrypted or not.

choices.text: Until the payment it was typed for has cleared at the bank
choices.why: Clearing the payment is when the rules say it must already be gone.

choices.text: For as long as the file holding it is encrypted at rest
choices.why: Encryption does not change it: the rule covers encrypted copies too.

prompt: Something identical on every call, such as the tool definitions or the temperature, is logged as a ___ to the configuration, and the configuration itself is kept once.
hint: A few bytes that point at the real thing.

prompt: Why does `guard scan` leave `123.456.789-00` in `rq-0004` unredacted?
hint: Look at what the CPF detector checks after the shape.

choices.text: It sits in the output, and the scanner reads only prompts
choices.why: The scanner reads both; this number matched in the prompt and in the output.

choices.text: Order numbers are on a list of formats the scanner knows to skip
choices.why: There is no such list. The arithmetic decides.

choices.text: Its check digits are wrong, so it is not a valid CPF
choices.why: Right: the shape matches and the arithmetic does not, so it is reported as LEAVE.

choices.text: Numbers written with dots are redacted only under --strict
choices.why: The dots make no difference; --strict drops the check-digit test, not a rule about dots.

prompt: Why redact as each record is written rather than in a nightly job over the log?
hint: Think about what happens to a log between being written and the night.

choices.text: A nightly job cannot read files that are still being appended to
choices.why: It can; the problem is what has already been copied by then.

choices.text: Backups and shipped logs made in between are never reached by the job
choices.why: Right: each of those is a copy of the unredacted text that the later job does not touch.

choices.text: Check digits can only be verified while the client's request is still open
choices.why: The check is arithmetic on the text and works at any time.

choices.text: The redacted tier cannot be written until the raw tier is deleted
choices.why: The two are written side by side; the raw tier is deleted by the sweep, later.

prompt: Which of these would the lab's detectors leave in the redacted tier? Choose all that apply.
hint: A pattern finds what has a pattern.

choices.text: A client's name and street address in a request for a bio
choices.why: Yes: no pattern recognises a name, and rq-0012 kept both.

choices.text: An e-mail address that the model repeats in its reply
choices.why: The scanner reads outputs as well as prompts, so it is redacted.

choices.text: A phone number written as 21 99876 5432
choices.why: Yes: the pattern expects a hyphen or nothing there, and rq-0022 kept it.

choices.text: The security code typed after a card number
choices.why: Yes: the number became [CARD] and CVV 123 stayed in rq-0005.

choices.text: An AWS access key pasted into the chat
choices.why: It has a fixed shape, and rq-0018 was redacted as [SECRET].

prompt: `guard scan` finds something in 11 of the 22 records, and `guard scan --strict` in 13. How many records does dropping the check digits add?
Tarefa sends its redacted tier to an outside analytics vendor and keeps it for 180 days. A colleague proposes --strict for that tier only. What is gained and what is lost?

choices.text: Mistyped CPFs stop reaching the vendor, and so do order numbers
choices.why: Right: every CPF shape goes, the valid and the mistyped, and the order numbers go with them.

choices.text: Nothing is lost, since strict mode only adds matches that pass the check digits
choices.why: It is the opposite: strict adds the matches that fail them.

choices.text: Names and addresses are removed as well, at the cost of more processing
choices.why: Strict changes the number detectors only. Names are still found by nothing.

choices.text: The raw tier becomes safe to keep for 180 days too
choices.why: The raw tier is not redacted at all, strict or not.

prompt: `guard sweep --check` exits 1 on Tarefa's machine. What does that tell the team?
hint: --check deletes nothing; it compares ages with limits.

choices.text: The sweep deleted a file that one of the holds should have protected
choices.why: --check reports what is still there, not what was removed.

choices.text: A hold has passed its end date and somebody needs to extend it
choices.why: An expired hold makes its file an ordinary overdue file; the exit code says nothing about holds.

choices.text: Files are past their limit: the sweep is failing or never ran
choices.why: Right: from the outside the two look the same, and this is the alarm for both.

choices.text: The policy file and the holds file contradict each other
choices.why: They cannot; a hold is an exception the policy reads.

prompt: Put the steps of bringing an existing log store under a retention policy in order.
hint: Nothing is deleted before somebody has read what would be.
items: Write a limit for each tier, with the purpose that sets it
Record the holds that open investigations need
Run the sweep with --dry-run and read what it would delete
Schedule the sweep, with --check beside it as the alarm

prompt: Match each field of an entry in `holds.json` to what it is for.
hint: One of the right-hand answers belongs to no field.

pairs.right: Which data the sweep must leave alone
The investigation the data is evidence for
Why it is kept, for whoever reads it next

right_distractors: Who is allowed to open the file

prompt: Before the sweep, `raw/2026-03-10.jsonl` is 204 days old and the raw tier's limit is 30. By how many days is it overdue?
Tarefa keeps nightly backups for 365 days, and the raw tier is in them. The sweep runs every night without fail. How long can a raw record actually survive?
hint: Where else does the record exist?

choices.text: Thirty days, because the sweep applies the policy every night
choices.why: The sweep deletes the file in the log store; the backups kept their copies.

choices.text: About a year, because the backups keep what the sweep deletes
choices.why: Right: the raw tier lives as long as the longest backup that contains it.

choices.text: Thirty days plus one night, until the next backup no longer contains it
choices.why: The next backup leaves it out, but the 364 earlier backups still hold it.

choices.text: Until the model provider deletes its own copy of the prompt
choices.why: The provider's copy is a separate one; this question is about Tarefa's own.

prompt: Which copies of a prompt does Tarefa's sweep leave untouched? Choose all that apply.
hint: The sweep deletes files in one directory.

choices.text: The copies inside the nightly backups
choices.why: Yes: a backup holds what the store held on the night it was taken.

choices.text: The redacted files older than 180 days
choices.why: Those are the sweep's own work; it deleted two of them.

choices.text: The text received by an observability vendor
choices.why: Yes: the vendor keeps it for its own period.

choices.text: The model provider's records of the calls
choices.why: Yes: those are governed by the provider's terms, and lesson 22 is about them.

prompt: Match each question to the tier at Tarefa that can answer it for the longest.
hint: The tier with the least in it that still answers.

pairs.left: Why did the assistant answer this client that way yesterday?
Did replies get worse after the August prompt change?
How many tokens did the chat surface use last year?

right_distractors: none: the question must not be logged

prompt: A client asks Tarefa to delete their data. Their calls appear in all three tiers. Which tiers does the request reach?
hint: Read what a metrics line contains.

choices.text: Only raw, since redaction removed the personal data from the other tier
choices.why: The redacted tier still names the account, and an account is a person.

choices.text: Raw and redacted, because both of them name the account and the metrics do not
choices.why: Right: the metrics line is a count per day and surface, with nobody in it.

choices.text: All three, because the metrics count this client's calls
choices.why: They count calls without saying whose; nothing in them leads back to the client.

choices.text: None, because logs kept for security are outside the request
choices.why: A security purpose may justify keeping some records, but it has to be argued; it does not put the logs outside the law.

prompt: A hold that names a file, a case and a reason but no ___ date is a second retention policy that nobody wrote down.
